description:
Jeni's ice cream is great and her ability to fight the big boys is something us smaller ice cream makers are keen to back but..... her Darkest Chocolate recipe is changing. 
In this video, we make our own version to capture the original essence of Jeni's Darkest Chocolate. 

What you'll need to make this extreme luxury chocolate ice cream:

250ml Milk
300ml Cream
120 Sugar
15g Dextrose
0.5 tsp Instant Coffee/Espresso powder
0.25 tsp Kosher Salt
50g of 70% Chocolate
3 tsp High Quality Cocoa Powder
10g Skimmed Milk Powder
1 tsp 100% Cocoa Powder (optional)
Monin Dark Chocolate Sauce
Additional 70% Chocolate for final batching

The 100% cocoa powder is optional as it only adds a little more depth of colour. 

If you want to make your Dark Chocolate Sauce, try this one from Michel Roux:
200g good-quality dark bitter chocolate, 70% cocoa solids
175ml milk
2 tbsp double cream
30g caster sugar
30g butter, diced
Chop the chocolate and place it in a heatproof bowl. Set over a pan of gently simmering water and allow to melt slowly, stirring occasionally until very smooth. Take off the heat.
Combine the milk, cream and sugar in a saucepan, stir with a whisk and bring to the boil.
Still stirring with the whisk, pour the boiling milk mixture onto the melted chocolate, then return the mixture to the pan and let it bubble over the heat for a few seconds, stirring continuously.
Turn off the heat and whisk in the butter, a little at a time, to give a smooth sauce. Pass it through a fine-meshed conical sieve. Serve at once or keep warm in a bain-marie.

comments.text: What cocoa powders do you use and what is the diff. From good quality cocoa powder and 100% cocoa powder.
comments.author: @lanawells6705

comments.text: I have over 30 different cocoa powders here at the moment. Good quality is like Ghirardelli, Cocoa Barry, Callebaut.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: ⁠ @PolarIceCreamery yes, I understand that, but is the 100% cocoa different from the first one in the recipe? Like maybe black cocoa powder? I use them all including the Rodell and a couple of others, so are you using 2 different cocoa powders? Sorry to keep bothering you!
comments.author: @lanawells6705

comments.text: @lanawells6705  the 100% is also sometimes called Black Cocoa. It adds a very bitter element to the ice cream. It’s easier control the bitterness by adding it like this as opposed to using all 100% as you couldn’t use much if you did that.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: @PolarIceCreamery  Thank you for clarifying! I very much appreciate all your hard work and expertise!
comments.author: @lanawells6705

comments.text: Sorry to be such a noob. I did "join" the channel because your content is so educational. It looks like you made a change to using grams at some point. Just to confirm my Google search, 250ml Milk = 250grams, 300ml Cream = 300grams? Thanks again for everything.
comments.author: @ChadSmithakaCCG

comments.text: Yep that’s right. All milk and cream weighs the same (basically) regardless of fat content.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: Despite my best efforts I am unable to understand the difference between the cocoa powders called for in the recipe. 3 tsp High Quality Cocoa Powder vs 1 tsp 100% Cocoa Powder (optional). Ghirardelli and Guittard are readily available in my area but I am not sure which of their products to get. Can anyone help?
comments.author: @ChadSmithakaCCG

comments.text: Use Ghirardelli dutched. The 100% is black cocoa powder and not required.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: Thank you. By the way, was the use of only 3 teaspoons of cocoa powder, which weighs around 7.38 grams, intentional? I’m surprised that the quantity is much less than what is used in Jeni’s cookbook

comments.text: Also must ice cream cookbooks give lame recipes with no imagination 😂✌️
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: Yeah it’s the combination of physical chocolate and cocoa that makes the difference here. The fat % is mostly cocoa solids instead of milk fat, this is why we can take it higher than normal. The cocoa powder is a color boost and flavor boost.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: Thank you again for your support 🙏
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.author: @roylee3196

comments.text: @PolarIceCreamery  I also input the ingredients into an ice cream calculator, and it showed a total fat content of 22.9% in the ice cream. Was this high fat percentage intentional?

comments.text: @roylee3196  lol yeah SUPER high fat , it works (it shouldn’t but it does). Saying that, it was with very high quality cream. I rarely not go that high here in Canada with their cream, it would super greasy. If you’re unsure, drop fat down to 16-18%.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: Hi Nick, did you forget to add the stabilisers to the ingredients list or they are not needed to this recipe? Thank you.
comments.author: @daniels2423

comments.text: With rich chocolate ice creams it’s best to deal with the sugar otherwise they freeze too hard. A stabilizer helps in every ice cream but high fat ones don’t benefit quite as much.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: @PolarIceCreamery  Thank you very for your reply. Really appreciate it. It's currently chilling in the fridge. Can't wait to see how it turns out.
comments.author: @daniels2423

comments.text: Nick. How do you decide when to use a stabilizer? Or when to use an emulsifier?
comments.author: @mohamedsharif9736

comments.text: Really, if you store it in the freezer for more than 24 hours, use a stabilizer. As for emulsifiers, some people prefer to use one every time. I’m in that group 90% of the time.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text:
@PolarIceCreamery  so follow up, how much stabilizer do you use? I’ve read some places where it’s 0.01-0.02% of weight. But I’m also guessing this is different for different stabilizers.

comments.text:

comments.text: @mohamedsharif9736  the fat content is more or less what’s makes and ice cream “creamy” although proper use of stabilizers can make it less important. Gelato is very low fat 6-10% range but have more stabilizers to account for that and the result is just as smooth.
